https://www.politico.eu/article/french-s.text: PARIS — French Socialist lawmaker Philippe Brun was barred Wednesday from running in an internal presidential primary over unspecified allegations against him that “may constitute a criminal offense.” “The national leadership of the Socialist Party was informed last night of facts that may constitute a criminal offense involving candidate Philippe Brun,” the center-left party said in a statement. “The Socialist Party does not compromise on the defense of women’s rights, nor on the exemplary conduct that must be its own,” the statement added. Brun was also provisionally suspended from the party. Advertisement Advertisement Though Brun was seen as an outsider, he had received enough endorsements from party leaders to run in the internal primary. The primary, whose first round will take place on Oct. 9 and 10, is being organized by the Socialist Party and its center-left allies with the aim of narrowing the field of social-democratic candidates down to one — thereby increasing the prospects of qualifying for the runoff in the French presidential election in May 2027. No Socialist candidate has achieved this since former President François Hollande in 2012. “I was stunned to learn this morning that I have been provisionally suspended from the Socialist Party and barred from running in the primary,” Brun said in a post on X , claiming that the allegations against him are tied to a dispute with a former female staffer. “I am unaware of these allegations. I do not know what I am being accused of.” MEP Rapha¨el Glucksmann is currently seen as the favorite in a center-left contest that has been marked by repeated infighting among the Socialists and their allies. Ségolène Royal, who was the Socialist candidate in 2007; Emmanuel Maurel, an independent lawmaker; and Jérôme Guedj, a member of the Socialist group in parliament, will also take part in the race. https://www.ibtimes.co.uk/tate-brothers-.text: Andrew and Tristan Tate will remain in federal custody in Miami after a US magistrate judge rejected their bid for release while they fight extradition to the UK.US Magistrate Judge Lauren Louis said the brothers' wealth and history of international travel made them 'quintessential flight risks', despite their lawyers arguing that their high public profiles would make it difficult for them to disappear.The decision keeps the controversial social media influencers in federal custody as they face a potentially lengthy extradition battle over criminal charges in Britain.The brothers, who hold both US and British citizenship, were arrested in Miami on 18 July after British authorities sought their extradition over allegations including rape, assault and facilitating trafficking for sexual exploitation, according to the Crown Prosecution Service. Both men deny wrongdoing.The ruling also comes as the brothers face separate legal problems in Romania. Romanian prosecutors have indicted Andrew Tate on charges including trafficking minors, money laundering, sex with a minor and witness tampering, while Tristan Tate was indicted for complicity.The developments leave the pair fighting legal proceedings across multiple countries while Britain prepares its full extradition request.Judge Says Tates Are 'Quintessential Flight Risks'In her ruling, Louis focused heavily on the brothers' ability to leave the United States if released. She said that, regardless of whether the extravagant wealth they have portrayed online is accurate, the evidence showed they had an 'exceptional capacity to flee the jurisdiction'.Prosecutors argued that the brothers should remain detained because extradition proceedings involving defendants with substantial international connections create a strong incentive to leave the country. They also raised concerns about the allegations against the pair and argued that releasing them could present a danger to the public.The defence argued that the brothers' 'extraordinary public visibility' would make fleeing impractical. They also characterised some of the brothers' online claims about wealth and luxury as theatrical and exaggerated.Full UK Extradition Request Due by 16 SeptemberThe immediate legal issue is not whether the Tates are guilty of the British allegations, but whether they meet the legal requirements for extradition to the UK to face those charges. The Crown Prosecution Service has authorised charges against Andrew and Tristan Tate involving alleged offences between July 2010 and August 2017.The CPS says the additional charges concern four further alleged victims and include rape, sexual assault, assault and arranging or facilitating trafficking for sexual exploitation. The CPS has stressed that the charging decisions are not findings of guilt and that the brothers are entitled to a fair trial.The Tates have not appeared in a British court to enter pleas to the charges. Britain has until 16 September to submit its full extradition request to the US State Department, according to court records cited by Reuters.The wider extradition process could take several months, meaning Wednesday's bail decision is unlikely to be the final major ruling before a potential extradition hearing.Romanian Indictment Adds Fresh Legal PressureThe brothers' UK extradition fight is unfolding alongside proceedings in Romania, where they have faced investigation since 2022.Reuters reported that Romanian prosecutors formally indicted Andrew Tate on 4 September on charges including trafficking minors, money laundering, sex with a minor and witness tampering.Tristan Tate was indicted for complicity. Their Romanian lawyer has rejected the allegations.The overlapping cases have become a central issue for the brothers' defence teams, which have argued that detention in the US complicates their ability to prepare for their Romanian proceedings.For now, however, the Miami ruling means the brothers will remain behind bars while the extradition process moves forward.Their lawyers have said they intend to continue defending them through the legal processes in each jurisdiction.

Poorvi Bondre, an editing student from Maharashtra and a member of the SRFTI student union, told DW that the event was affiliated with the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS) and was being used to promote its agenda on campus. She said students had opposed the meeting because it was not a film screening but what she described as direct RSS promotion. The RSS is a right-wing Hindu organization and the ideological parent of Prime Minister Narendra Modi's ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) . "This was an RSS event. We were completely unaware of this event. When we asked them what this was about, the fight started," Bondre said. "They called us anti-nationals and Naxals and attacked us with knives." Videos of the incident have circulated on social media, showing students with what appear to be knife wounds. However, DW could not independently verify their authenticity. https://www.forbes.ro/adrian-gociu-manag.text: The risks of investing in Romania are not a reason to stay away, but something that can be identified, priced and covered by contract. The condition is properly conducted due diligence, which many entrepreneurs and investors still overlook. The message came from Adrian Gociu, Managing Partner at Gociu Lawyers, at Forbes România Business Bridges 2026, the event organized by Forbes Romania at Forbes on Fifth in New York. "Investing without due diligence, you buy what the seller can tell you. Investing with due diligence, you buy what is actually there," Adrian Gociu said. The lawyer says that "in business, there is no risk mitigation that can stop every risk, and certainty is only a desire. The standard is to mitigate most of the risks, and only then can we talk about certainty." Gociu listed several vulnerabilities of the Romanian market. The first concerns the way companies are built: many large firms are owned directly by their founders, as individuals, without holding companies or a clear corporate architecture. The second concerns intellectual property. "Around 70% of companies operate without formal IP protection. We consider it a structural gap," the lawyer said. "Taxes are growing, and maybe they will grow a little more. But it's not only a Romanian problem, fiscal instability happens in all countries of the world," Gociu observed. Insolvencies are a warning sign. Their number already rose in 2025 and is set to remain high, and many companies look solid only on paper. Gociu does not, however, advise investors to avoid them automatically. "You have to check everything about your partners, to know exactly who they are and why they entered insolvency. Because they may be a very good partner, even if they had problems," the lawyer explained. This leads to the distinction he considers essential: business due diligence and partner due diligence. "Partner due diligence is very important and it's a new subject, because in general everybody does due diligence on the business and not on the partner. I believe a good business works with a good partner," Gociu said. The checks cover the control structure, VAT status, tax position, solvency, litigation, track record, exposure to international sanctions and market reputation. "History can tell us part of what will happen in the future," he added. Whatever due diligence uncovers must then be reflected in the price and in the contract. Every risk has a clause, from fiscal instability and change-of-law clauses and tax indemnities, to price adjustment mechanisms, audit rights and termination for breach. "Every risk can be managed and mitigated with the right clause and good due diligence," Gociu said. The last layer of protection is structuring, and here his message was aimed at Romanian entrepreneurs. "Many Romanian companies are run by individuals, by their founders, who have not built holdings or a corporate architecture. I believe it is very important for them to start creating holdings and separating risks, in order to prepare for a sale or to attract investors," the lawyer explained. "Risks are not a problem. Romania is not a problem, it is a very good country to invest in. But we have to check every risk, and due diligence is very important," Adrian Gociu concluded.
